name: Ethics and Bias Audit Projects
title: Ethics and Bias Audit Projects
answer: Ethics and bias audit projects have students test real AI tools with carefully chosen inputs to see whether the tools treat different groups differently, then write up findings and propose fixes. They matter because they teach students that AI tools are made by people, can be questioned, and can be improved. The work is feasible for older students, with middle school research showing they can handle it and high school students able to go further.

sections.body: A bias audit project asks students to probe an AI tool rather than simply use it. Students choose inputs designed to reveal whether the tool responds differently to different groups, for example checking whether an image generator shows only certain kinds of people when asked for a doctor or an engineer. They then document what they found and suggest how the tool or its use could be changed. The idea solves the problem that students often meet AI as a neutral black box, and it gives them a concrete way to examine fairness claims instead of accepting them. It also turns ethics from an abstract topic into an investigation students carry out themselves.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In middle school, the text describes students learning how machine learning works, identifying bias in AI systems, suggesting ways to reduce it, and connecting AI to future careers. Researchers who built three AI and ethics curricula for middle school found that trained teachers could teach them well when active learning was used and ethics was woven into technical lessons. High school students can take the same ideas further, running fuller audits and writing up findings with proposed fixes. Across grade bands, the teacher reviews the plan before students begin. Students work only with approved tools that meet age limits, remove personal information from their tests, and avoid generating harmful content even for study.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this work as research from middle schools. In one workshop, middle school students learned how machine learning works, identified bias in AI systems, suggested ways to reduce it, and connected AI to future careers (Zhang et al., 2023). Researchers who built three AI and ethics curricula for middle school found that trained teachers could teach them well using active learning and ethics woven into technical lessons (Williams et al., 2023). The text adds that high school students can take the same ideas further.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Bias audits must use tools that meet student age limits, so approved tools are the starting point rather than any tool students find. Students should remove any personal information from their tests and should avoid generating harmful content even when the purpose is to study it. The teacher reviews the plan before students begin, which keeps the decision about what is acceptable with a person rather than with the students alone or the tool. The text frames these projects as careful work that, done well, teaches students that AI tools are made by people and can be questioned and improved.
